meta.title: Quantum Mechanics I — Module III: Mathematical Tools of Quantum Mechanics
meta.subject: Quantum Mechanics I (MAT/PHY, Sem 5)

glossary.definition: A linear vector space is a set of vectors and a set of scalars closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.
glossary.example: In Section 2.2.1, any linear combination \(a\psi + b\phi\) of two vectors \(\psi\) and \(\phi\) is another vector in the same space.

glossary.definition: The scalar product \((\psi, \phi)\) is a rule that pairs two vectors of a Hilbert space to give a complex number with \((\psi, \phi) = (\phi, \psi)^*\).
glossary.example: In Equation (2.21), the scalar product of two functions is \((\psi, \phi) = \int \psi^*(x)\phi(x)\,dx\).

glossary.definition: A Cauchy sequence is a sequence of vectors \(\psi_n\) whose distance \(\|\psi_n - \psi_m\|\) approaches zero as \(n, m \to \infty\).
glossary.example: Equation (2.9) writes the Cauchy condition as \(\lim_{n,m\to\infty} \|\psi_n - \psi_m\| = 0\).

glossary.definition: A Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\) is a linear vector space with a strictly positive scalar product that is both separable and complete.
glossary.example: Square-integrable wave functions \(\psi(\vec{r}, t)\) form an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.

glossary.definition: The dual Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}_d\) is the partner vector space whose elements (bras) pair with vectors of \(\mathcal{H}\) (kets) to form scalar products.
glossary.example: In \((\phi, \psi)\) or \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\), \(\psi\) belongs to \(\mathcal{H}\) while \(\phi\) belongs to \(\mathcal{H}_d\).

glossary.definition: A set of nonzero vectors \(\phi_1, \dots, \phi_N\) is linearly independent if \(\sum_{i=1}^N a_i\phi_i = 0\) holds only when every scalar \(a_i = 0\).
glossary.example: In Example 2.1(a), \(f(x) = 4\), \(g(x) = x^2\), and \(h(x) = e^{2x}\) are linearly independent on the real \(x\)-axis.

glossary.definition: A basis is a maximum set of linearly independent vectors \(\{\phi_i\}\) that spans the vector space so any vector expands as \(\psi = \sum_i a_i\phi_i\).
glossary.example: The unit vectors \(\vec{i}, \vec{j}, \vec{k}\) form an orthonormal basis of three-dimensional Euclidean space.

glossary.definition: The dimension of a vector space is the maximum number of linearly independent vectors that the space can have.
glossary.example: Euclidean space has dimension 3, whereas the Hilbert space of wave functions has infinite dimension.

glossary.definition: A function \(\psi(x)\) is square-integrable if the integral of its modulus squared \((\psi, \psi) = \int |\psi(x)|^2\,dx\) is finite.
glossary.example: By Equation (2.23), any physical wave function satisfies \(\int |\psi(\vec{r}, t)|^2\,d^3r = 1\) and is square-integrable.

glossary.definition: A ket \(|\psi\rangle\) is Dirac's symbol for a quantum state vector belonging to the Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\), independent of any coordinate system.
glossary.example: In a discrete basis, a ket \(|\psi\rangle\) is represented by a column vector of its components \(a_n = \langle\phi_n|\psi\rangle\).

glossary.definition: A bra \(\langle\psi|\) is Dirac's symbol for an element of the dual space \(\mathcal{H}_d\), uniquely paired with the ket \(|\psi\rangle\).
glossary.example: In Example 2.3, the ket \(|\phi\rangle\) has the corresponding row bra \(\langle\phi| = (2\ \ i\ \ 2+3i)\).

glossary.definition: A bra-ket \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\) is Dirac's notation for the scalar product of the bra \(\langle\phi|\) with the ket \(|\psi\rangle\).
glossary.example: For normalized states, \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\) is the probability amplitude to find state \(|\psi\rangle\) in state \(|\phi\rangle\).

glossary.definition: The Schwarz inequality states that for any two states \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\), \(|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2 \le \langle\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\phi|\phi\rangle\).
glossary.example: Equation (2.34) becomes an equality when \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\) are proportional: \(|\psi\rangle = \alpha|\phi\rangle\).

glossary.definition: Two states \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\) are orthogonal if their scalar product vanishes, \(\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = 0\), and orthonormal if each also has unit norm.
glossary.example: Equation (2.38): \(\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = 0\), \(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle = 1\), and \(\langle\phi|\phi\rangle = 1\).

glossary.definition: An operator \(\hat{A}\) is a mathematical rule that transforms a ket \(|\psi\rangle\) into another ket \(|\psi'\rangle = \hat{A}|\psi\rangle\) in the same space.
glossary.example: In Equation (2.56), a linear operator obeys \(\hat{A}(a_1|\psi_1\rangle + a_2|\psi_2\rangle) = a_1\hat{A}|\psi_1\rangle + a_2\hat{A}|\psi_2\rangle\).

glossary.definition: The Hermitian adjoint \(\hat{A}^\dagger\) of an operator \(\hat{A}\) is defined by \(\langle\psi|\hat{A}^\dagger|\phi\rangle = \langle\phi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle^*\) for all states.
glossary.example: For a matrix \(A\), the adjoint \(A^\dagger = (A^T)^*\) is formed by transposing rows and columns and taking complex conjugates.

glossary.definition: An operator \(\hat{A}\) is Hermitian if it equals its own adjoint, \(\hat{A} = \hat{A}^\dagger\), and anti-Hermitian if \(\hat{B}^\dagger = -\hat{B}\).
glossary.example: By Equation (2.74), the expectation value \(\langle\psi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle\) of a Hermitian operator is always a real number.

glossary.definition: The commutator of two operators \(\hat{A}\) and \(\hat{B}\) is their order difference \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A}\).
glossary.example: Position and momentum obey the canonical commutator \([\hat{X}, \hat{P}_x] = i\hbar\hat{I}\) in Equation (2.83).

glossary.definition: The anticommutator of two operators \(\hat{A}\) and \(\hat{B}\) is the symmetric sum \(\{\hat{A}, \hat{B}\} = \hat{A}\hat{B} + \hat{B}\hat{A}\).
glossary.example: Equation (2.80) defines \(\{\hat{A}, \hat{B}\} = \hat{A}\hat{B} + \hat{B}\hat{A}\).

glossary.definition: The uncertainty relation between two Hermitian operators \(\hat{A}\) and \(\hat{B}\) states that \(\Delta A\,\Delta B \ge \frac{1}{2}|\langle[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]\rangle|\).
glossary.example: Applying Equation (2.106) to \(\hat{X}\) and \(\hat{P}_x\) gives Heisenberg's relation \(\Delta x\,\Delta p_x \ge \hbar/2\).

glossary.definition: A function of a linear operator \(F(\hat{A})\) is defined by its Taylor power series expansion \(F(\hat{A}) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n \hat{A}^n\).
glossary.example: Equation (2.109) defines the exponential operator \(e^{a\hat{A}} = \hat{I} + a\hat{A} + \frac{a^2}{2!}\hat{A}^2 + \cdots\).

glossary.definition: An eigenvector \(|\psi\rangle\) of \(\hat{A}\) is a state that \(\hat{A}\) merely scales by a complex number \(a\), called the eigenvalue: \(\hat{A}|\psi\rangle = a|\psi\rangle\).
glossary.example: By Theorem 2.1, every eigenvalue \(a_n\) of a Hermitian operator is a real number.

glossary.definition: An eigenvalue is degenerate if two or more linearly independent eigenvectors share that same eigenvalue.
glossary.example: If five linearly independent eigenvectors share one eigenvalue, that eigenvalue is fivefold degenerate.

glossary.definition: The completeness (or closure) relation states that summing the outer products of all orthonormal basis kets gives the unit operator: \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |\phi_n\rangle\langle\phi_n| = \hat{I}\).
glossary.example: Inserting \(\hat{I} = \sum_n |\phi_n\rangle\langle\phi_n|\) expands any ket as \(|\psi\rangle = \sum_n \langle\phi_n|\psi\rangle|\phi_n\rangle\).

glossary.definition: The trace \(\text{Tr}(\hat{A})\) of an operator is the sum of its diagonal matrix elements \(\sum_n \langle\phi_n|\hat{A}|\phi_n\rangle = \sum_n A_{nn}\) in any orthonormal basis.
glossary.example: By Equation (2.210), the trace of any commutator vanishes: \(\text{Tr}([\hat{A}, \hat{B}]) = 0\).

glossary.definition: A unitary transformation is a change of orthonormal basis given by a matrix \(U\) with \(U_{mn} = \langle\phi'_m|\phi_n\rangle\) satisfying \(U^\dagger U = U U^\dagger = I\).
glossary.example: Under a change of basis, kets transform as \(|\psi_{\text{new}}\rangle = \hat{U}|\psi_{\text{old}}\rangle\) and operators as \(\hat{A}_{\text{new}} = \hat{U}\hat{A}_{\text{old}}\hat{U}^\dagger\).

glossary.definition: The secular (or characteristic) equation is the determinant condition \(\det(A_{mn} - a\delta_{nm}) = 0\) whose roots are the eigenvalues \(a_n\) of \(\hat{A}\).
glossary.example: For an \(N \times N\) matrix \(A\), solving \(\det(A - aI) = 0\) yields the spectrum \(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_N\).

glossary.definition: The Dirac delta function \(\delta(x - x_0)\) is a generalized function that vanishes for \(x \ne x_0\) and sifts out \(f(x_0)\) under integration: \(\int f(x)\delta(x-x_0)\,dx = f(x_0)\).
glossary.example: Equation (2.275) expresses continuous basis orthonormality as \(\langle\chi_k|\chi_{k'}\rangle = \delta(k' - k)\).

glossary.definition: The position representation expands states in the continuous eigenkets \(\{|\vec{r}\rangle\}\) of \(\hat{\vec{R}}\), where the component \(\langle\vec{r}|\psi\rangle = \psi(\vec{r})\) is the spatial wave function.
glossary.example: In the position representation, the momentum operator acts as the gradient \(\hat{\vec{P}} = -i\hbar\vec{\nabla}\).

glossary.definition: The momentum representation expands states in the continuous eigenkets \(\{|\vec{p}\rangle\}\) of \(\hat{\vec{P}}\), where \(\langle\vec{p}|\psi\rangle = \Psi(\vec{p})\) is the momentum wave function.
glossary.example: In the momentum representation, the position operator acts as \(\hat{R}_j = i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial p_j}\).

glossary.definition: Matrix mechanics is Heisenberg's formulation of quantum mechanics in a discrete basis, where observables are matrices and \(\hat{H}|\psi\rangle = E|\psi\rangle\) is a matrix eigenvalue problem.
glossary.example: Diagonalizing the Hamiltonian matrix in Equation (2.352) yields the energy levels \(E_n\).

glossary.definition: Wave mechanics is Schrödinger's formulation of quantum mechanics in the continuous position basis, where \(\hat{H}|\psi\rangle = E|\psi\rangle\) becomes a differential equation for \(\psi(\vec{r})\).
glossary.example: Equation (2.354): \(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\psi(\vec{r}) + \hat{V}(\vec{r})\psi(\vec{r}) = E\psi(\vec{r})\).

cards.title: Why whole functions can behave like arrows in space
cards.meaning: A linear vector space is any collection of objects that you can add together and multiply by numbers while staying inside the collection.

cards.picture: Just as two arrows add to make a new arrow on the left, two wave functions add to make a new wave function on the right.
cards.example: Adding 2 times sin(x) and 3 times cos(x) gives 2 sin(x) + 3 cos(x), which is still a smooth wave function.
cards.bridge: Section 2.2.1 formalizes this with two sets (vectors and scalars) obeying closure, addition, and scalar multiplication rules.

cards.title: What is a linear vector space?
cards.body: A linear vector space is a set of vectors \(\psi, \phi, \chi, \dots\) and scalars \(a, b, c, \dots\) closed under commutative, associative vector addition (with zero \(O\) and inverse \(-\psi\)) and distributive scalar multiplication.
cards.tex: a(\psi + \phi) = a\psi + a\phi, \quad (a + b)\psi = a\psi + b\psi, \quad a(b\psi) = (ab)\psi, \quad I\psi = \psi

cards.title: What turns a vector space into a Hilbert space
cards.meaning: A Hilbert space is a vector space equipped with a complex dot product (scalar product) to measure lengths and angles, plus no missing limit points.

cards.picture: Every Cauchy sequence ψ₁, ψ₂, ψ₃, ... inside the shaded Hilbert space H converges to a limit ψ that stays inside H.
cards.example: For a particle on a line, the collection of all square-integrable functions ψ(x) is a Hilbert space, even before normalizing them to 1.
cards.bridge: Section 2.2.2 defines H by four properties: linearity, a strictly positive scalar product, separability, and completeness.

cards.title: What are a Hilbert space and its scalar product?
cards.body: A Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\) is a linear space with a strictly positive scalar product \((\psi,\phi) = (\phi,\psi)^*\) (linear in the second factor, antilinear in the first, \(\in \mathcal{H}_d\)) that is separable and complete in norm \(\|\psi\|^2 = (\psi,\psi)\).

cards.title: What are linear independence, dimension, and basis?
cards.body: Nonzero vectors \(\{\phi_i\}\) are linearly independent if \(\sum_{i=1}^N a_i\phi_i = 0\) implies all \(a_i = 0\); the maximum number \(N\) is the dimension, and a complete orthonormal basis \((\phi_i,\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}\) expands any \(\psi\).

cards.title: What is a square-integrable wave function?
cards.body: In function space, the scalar product is \((\psi,\phi) = \int \psi^*(x)\phi(x)\,dx\), and \(\psi(x)\) is square-integrable if \((\psi,\psi) = \int |\psi(x)|^2\,dx\) is finite; physical wave functions obey Equation (2.23).

cards.label: Example 2.1(b) · §2.2.3
cards.title: Testing linear independence of x, x², x³ (Equation (2.14))
cards.legend: \(f(x)=x,\ g(x)=x^2,\ h(x)=x^3\) functions on the real \(x\)-axis, \(a_1, a_2, a_3\) scalar coefficients.

phases.name: Linear combination
phases.why: set a₁f(x) + a₂g(x) + a₃h(x) equal to zero for all x

phases.name: Sample x = ±1
phases.why: evaluate at x = -1 and x = 1 to relate the coefficients

phases.name: Sample x = 3
phases.why: use x = 3 in Equation (2.14) to eliminate a₁ and a₃

steps.note: Start with Equation (2.11) applied to \(f(x)=x,\ g(x)=x^2,\ h(x)=x^3\) for all real \(x\).

ask.q: In Example 2.1(b), what do we obtain by evaluating at \(x = -1\)?
ask.why: Substituting x = -1 gives a₁(-1) + a₂(-1)² + a₃(-1)³ = -a₁ + a₂ - a₃ = 0.

steps.note: First equation in Equation (2.14) from setting \(x = -1\).
Second equation in Equation (2.14) from setting \(x = 1\).

ask.q: Adding \(-a_1 + a_2 - a_3 = 0\) and \(a_1 + a_2 + a_3 = 0\) gives what?
ask.why: Adding the two equations cancels ±a₁ and ±a₃, leaving 2a₂ = 0 and hence a₂ = 0.

steps.note: Adding the \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\) equations yields \(a_2 = 0\) and \(a_1 + a_3 = 0\).

ask.q: What is the third equation in Equation (2.14) at \(x = 3\)?
ask.why: Substituting x = 3 into a₁x + a₂x² + a₃x³ = 0 gives 3a₁ + 9a₂ + 27a₃ = 0.

ask.q: What does \(24a_3 = 0\) imply for \(a_1, a_2, a_3\)?
ask.why: Since 24a₃ = 0 gives a₃ = 0 and a₁ = -a₃ = 0, we have a₁ = a₂ = a₃ = 0, proving linear independence.

steps.note: Since \(a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = 0\), the functions \(x, x^2, x^3\) are linearly independent.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In a Hilbert space, how does the scalar product \((a\phi_1 + b\phi_2, \psi)\) expand?
cards.why: By Equation (2.6), the scalar product in a Hilbert space is antilinear with respect to the first factor, pulling out complex conjugates a* and b*.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 2.1(c), why are \(f(x)=x,\ g(x)=5x,\ h(x)=x^2\) linearly dependent?
options: Because their scalar product is zero
cards.why: One function can be written as a linear combination of the others with not all scalars zero: g(x) = 5f(x) + 0·h(x).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Every Cauchy sequence in a Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\) converges to an element of \(\mathcal{H}\) because \(\mathcal{H}\) is ______.
cards.why: By property (d) in Section 2.2.2, completeness means that every Cauchy sequence in H converges to a unique limit inside H.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the dimension of the Hilbert space of square-integrable wave functions?
cards.why: As stated in Section 2.2.4, the Hilbert space of square-integrable functions has infinite dimension because expanding a wave function requires infinitely many basis functions.

cards.title: Freeing quantum state vectors from coordinates
cards.meaning: Dirac's ket |ψ⟩ is a coordinate-free symbol for a quantum state, paired with a dual bra ⟨φ| so their bracket ⟨φ|ψ⟩ gives the scalar product.

cards.picture: A row bra ⟨φ| on the left and a column ket |ψ⟩ in the middle snap together into the scalar bra-ket ⟨φ|ψ⟩ on the right.
cards.example: Just as an arrow A exists before choosing x, y, z axes, the state ket |ψ⟩ exists before choosing position ψ(r,t) or momentum ψ(p,t).
cards.bridge: Section 2.3 defines kets |ψ⟩ in H, bras ⟨ψ| in H_d, and the bra-ket scalar product ⟨φ|ψ⟩ in Equation (2.24).

cards.title: What are kets, bras, and bra-kets?
cards.body: A ket \(|\psi\rangle \in \mathcal{H}\) is a coordinate-free state vector, a bra \(\langle\psi| \in \mathcal{H}_d\) is its unique dual partner, and the bra-ket \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\) is their scalar product.
cards.tex: a|\psi\rangle + b|\phi\rangle \longleftrightarrow a^*\langle\psi| + b^*\langle\phi|, \qquad \langle\phi|\psi\rangle = \int \phi^*(\vec{r}, t)\psi(\vec{r}, t)\,d^3r

cards.title: What are the Schwarz and triangle inequalities?
cards.body: Any two states obey the Schwarz inequality \(|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2 \le \langle\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\phi|\phi\rangle\) and triangle inequality; they are orthogonal if \(\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = 0\) and orthonormal if also unit norm.

cards.label: Example 2.3 · §2.3
cards.title: Bra and scalar product of column kets
cards.body: In Example 2.3, transposing and conjugating \(|\phi\rangle\) gives the row bra \(\langle\phi| = (2\ \ i\ \ 2+3i)\) (Equation (2.39)), and row-by-column multiplication gives \(7 + 8i\) (Equation (2.40)).

cards.label: Example 2.4 · §2.3
cards.title: Bra-ket algebra & Schwarz inequality (Equations (2.43)–(2.47))

phases.name: Dual bra
phases.why: form ⟨ψ| by conjugating coefficients of |ψ⟩

phases.name: Scalar product
phases.why: evaluate ⟨ψ|χ⟩ using orthonormality ⟨φ_i|φ_j⟩ = δ_ij

phases.name: Norms & Schwarz test
phases.why: compare |⟨ψ|χ⟩|² with ⟨ψ|ψ⟩⟨χ|χ⟩ in Equation (2.47)

steps.note: Take complex conjugates of \(3i\) and \(-7i\) in \(|\psi\rangle = 3i|\phi_1\rangle - 7i|\phi_2\rangle\).

ask.q: Using \(\langle\phi_1|\phi_1\rangle = \langle\phi_2|\phi_2\rangle = 1\) and \(\langle\phi_1|\phi_2\rangle = 0\), what is \(\langle\psi|\chi\rangle\)?
ask.why: Orthonormality eliminates the cross terms ⟨φ₁|φ₂⟩ and ⟨φ₂|φ₁⟩, leaving (-3i)(-1)⟨φ₁|φ₁⟩ + (7i)(2i)⟨φ₂|φ₂⟩.

ask.q: What is the modulus squared \(|\langle\psi|\chi\rangle|^2\) of \(\langle\psi|\chi\rangle = -14 + 3i\)?
ask.why: For any complex number x + iy, the modulus squared is x² + y² = (-14)² + 3² = 196 + 9 = 205.

steps.note: Square the modulus of \(\langle\psi|\chi\rangle = -14 + 3i\) to get \(14^2 + 3^2 = 205\).

ask.q: What are the norms \(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\) and \(\langle\chi|\chi\rangle\) in Equations (2.45)–(2.46)?

steps.note: Multiply \(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle = 58\) and \(\langle\chi|\chi\rangle = 5\) to get \(290\) (Equation (2.47)).

ask.q: How do \(|\langle\psi|\chi\rangle|^2 = 205\) and \(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\chi|\chi\rangle = 290\) confirm the Schwarz inequality?
ask.why: Because 205 < (58)(5) = 290, the Schwarz inequality (2.34) holds strictly (Equation (2.47)).

steps.note: Since \(290 - 205 = 85 > 0\), the Schwarz inequality \(|\langle\psi|\chi\rangle|^2 \le \langle\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\chi|\chi\rangle\) is satisfied.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the bra corresponding to the ket \(a|\psi\rangle + b|\phi\rangle\)?
cards.why: By Equation (2.27), replacing kets with bras requires taking the complex conjugates of the scalar coefficients a and b.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When does the Schwarz inequality \(|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2 \le \langle\psi|\psi\rangle\langle\phi|\phi\rangle\) become an equality?
options: Only when both states are zero
cards.why: As stated below Equation (2.34), the Schwarz inequality becomes an equality when |ψ⟩ and |φ⟩ are linearly dependent (proportional: |ψ⟩ = α|φ⟩).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For normalized states \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\), what does \(\langle\phi|\psi\rangle\) represent physically?
cards.why: By Born's probabilistic interpretation in Section 2.3, ⟨φ|ψ⟩ is the probability amplitude that a system in state |ψ⟩ is found in state |φ⟩ upon measurement.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: Two kets \(|\psi\rangle\) and \(|\phi\rangle\) are said to be ______ if \(\langle\psi|\phi\rangle = 0\) and \(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle = \langle\phi|\phi\rangle = 1\).
cards.why: By Equation (2.38), states that are mutually orthogonal and each normalized to unit norm are called orthonormal.

cards.title: An operator as a machine that turns one state vector into another
cards.meaning: An operator Â is a mathematical rule that acts on a ket |ψ⟩ from the left to produce a new ket |ψ'⟩ = Â|ψ⟩ in the same space.

cards.picture: An operator Â takes an input ket |ψ⟩ on the left and outputs a transformed ket |ψ'⟩ = Â|ψ⟩ on the right.
cards.example: For a 2-entry column ket, a 2×2 matrix acts as a linear operator; for a wave function ψ(r), the gradient ∇ acts as a linear operator.
cards.bridge: Section 2.4.1 defines operators on kets and bras in Equation (2.51), linear operators in Equation (2.56), and expectation values in Equation (2.58).

cards.title: What is a linear operator and its expectation value?
cards.body: An operator \(\hat{A}\) maps \(\hat{A}|\psi\rangle = |\psi'\rangle\) and \(\langle\phi|\hat{A} = \langle\phi'|\); it is linear if \(\hat{A}(a_1|\psi_1\rangle + a_2|\psi_2\rangle) = a_1\hat{A}|\psi_1\rangle + a_2\hat{A}|\psi_2\rangle\), with expectation value \(\langle\hat{A}\rangle = \langle\psi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle/\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\).

cards.title: Why quantum observables use Hermitian operators
cards.meaning: Taking the Hermitian adjoint reverses a product and conjugates scalars, and an operator that equals its own adjoint (Â = Â†) is called Hermitian.
cards.art: <svg viewBox="0 0 260 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="22" y="36" width="96" height="68" class="s ok"/><rect x="142" y="36" width="96" height="68" class="s ok"/><line x1="118" y1="70" x2="142" y2="70" class="lk"/><text x="70" y="58" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Matrix A</text><text x="70" y="80" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(1    −i)</text><text x="70" y="96" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(i    −1)</text><text x="190" y="58" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Adjoint A† = (A^T)*</text><text x="190" y="80" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(1    −i)</text><text x="190" y="96" text-anchor="middle" class="t">(i    −1)</text><text x="130" y="132" text-anchor="middle" class="t">Here A† = A (Hermitian):</text><text x="130" y="152" text-anchor="middle" class="t">⟨ψ|Â|ψ⟩ = ⟨ψ|Â|ψ⟩* is always real</text></svg>
cards.picture: Swapping rows and columns of the 2×2 matrix A and taking complex conjugates leaves A unchanged, so A† = A.
cards.example: For the 2×2 matrix with diagonal (1, -1) and off-diagonal (-i, i), transposing swaps -i and i, and conjugating restores (-i, i).
cards.bridge: Section 2.4.2 defines the Hermitian adjoint by ⟨ψ|Â†|φ⟩ = ⟨φ|Â|ψ⟩* in Equation (2.60) and Hermitian operators by Â = Â† in Equation (2.70).

cards.title: What is the Hermitian adjoint and its conjugate rule?
cards.body: The Hermitian adjoint \(\hat{A}^\dagger\) satisfies \(\langle\psi|\hat{A}^\dagger|\phi\rangle = \langle\phi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle^*\); to take the adjoint of any product, reverse factor order, conjugate scalars, swap kets and bras, and take operator adjoints.

cards.title: What are Hermitian and anti-Hermitian operators?
cards.body: An operator is Hermitian if \(\hat{A} = \hat{A}^\dagger\) (so \(\langle\psi|\hat{A}|\phi\rangle = \langle\phi|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle^*\)) and skew-Hermitian (or anti-Hermitian) if \(\hat{B}^\dagger = -\hat{B}\).

ask.why: By Equations (2.61) and (2.64), (Â + Â†)† = Â† + (Â†)† = Â† + Â = B̂, so B̂ is always Hermitian.

ask.q: By Equation (2.60), what is \(\langle\psi|\hat{A}^\dagger|\psi\rangle\) for any state \(|\psi\rangle\)?
ask.why: Setting |φ⟩ = |ψ⟩ in Equation (2.60) gives ⟨ψ|Â†|ψ⟩ = ⟨ψ|Â|ψ⟩*.

ask.why: Replacing B̂† by −B̂ inside ⟨ψ|B̂†|ψ⟩ gives −⟨ψ|B̂|ψ⟩.

ask.q: If a complex number \(z\) satisfies \(z = -z^*\), what kind of number is \(z\)?
ask.why: Writing z = x + iy gives x + iy = -x + iy, so 2x = 0 and z = iy is purely imaginary.

steps.note: The real part vanishes, proving that \(\langle\psi|\hat{B}|\psi\rangle\) is purely imaginary.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When the product \(\hat{A}\hat{B}\hat{C}\hat{D}\) acts on a ket \(|\psi\rangle\), which operator acts first?
cards.why: As stated below Equation (2.55), the operator closest to the ket acts first: D̂ acts on |ψ⟩ first, then Ĉ, then B̂, and finally Â.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Equation (2.67), what is the Hermitian adjoint of the outer-product operator \(|\psi\rangle\langle\phi|\)?
cards.why: Reversing the order and swapping ket and bra gives (|ψ⟩⟨φ|)† = (⟨φ|)†(|ψ⟩)† = |φ⟩⟨ψ| (Equation (2.67)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In Example 2.6(a), for any operator \(\hat{A}\), what kind of operator is \(i(\hat{A} - \hat{A}^\dagger)\)?
cards.why: Taking the adjoint gives [i(Â − Â†)]† = −i(Â† − Â) = i(Â − Â†), so it equals its own adjoint and is Hermitian.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: By Equation (2.74), the expectation value of a Hermitian operator is always a ______ number.
cards.why: Because ⟨ψ|Â|ψ⟩ = ⟨ψ|Â|ψ⟩* when Â† = Â, the expectation value of any Hermitian operator is real.

cards.meaning: The commutator [Â, B̂] = ÂB̂ − B̂Â compares doing B̂ then Â against doing Â then B̂.

cards.title: What are the commutator and anticommutator?
cards.body: The commutator is \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A}\) and the anticommutator is \(\{\hat{A}, \hat{B}\} = \hat{A}\hat{B} + \hat{B}\hat{A}\); two operators commute if \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = 0\).

objects.text: Eq. (2.82): Hermitian Â, B̂ have Hermitian ÂB̂ iff [Â, B̂] = 0
objects.name: comm

cards.title: Properties of commutators (Equations (2.84)–(2.92))
cards.body: Commutators are antisymmetric, linear, obey product distributivity \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}\hat{C}] = [\hat{A}, \hat{B}]\hat{C} + \hat{B}[\hat{A}, \hat{C}]\), satisfy the Jacobi identity, and vanish with any scalar \([\hat{A}, b] = 0\).

ask.why: Taking the Hermitian adjoint reverses the order of each product, giving B̂†Â† − Â†B̂†.

cards.q: If \(\hat{A}\) and \(\hat{B}\) are Hermitian, when is their product \(\hat{A}\hat{B}\) also Hermitian?
cards.why: By Equation (2.82), (ÂB̂)† = B̂†Â† = B̂Â, so (ÂB̂)† = ÂB̂ holds if and only if ÂB̂ = B̂Â, i.e., [Â, B̂] = 0.

cards.title: How non-commuting operators force a minimum spread product
cards.meaning: Whenever two Hermitian operators do not commute, their measurement spreads ΔA and ΔB in state |ψ⟩ obey ΔA ΔB ≥ ½|⟨[Â, B̂]⟩|.

cards.picture: Applying the Schwarz inequality to the deviation states |χ⟩ = ΔÂ|ψ⟩ and |φ⟩ = ΔB̂|ψ⟩ bounds ΔA ΔB from below by ½|⟨[Â, B̂]⟩|.
cards.example: Using our 2×2 matrices A = ((1,0),(0,-1)) and B = ((0,1),(1,0)) on |ψ⟩ = (1/√2)(1, i)^T gives ⟨[A,B]⟩ = -2i, so ΔA ΔB ≥ 1.
cards.bridge: Section 2.4.5 proves the general relation Equation (2.106) and applies it to [X̂, P̂_x] = iħÎ to get Heisenberg's relation Equation (2.107).

cards.title: What are operator deviations and uncertainties?
cards.body: For a Hermitian operator \(\hat{A}\) in a normalized state \(|\psi\rangle\), the deviation operator is \(\Delta\hat{A} = \hat{A} - \langle\hat{A}\rangle\) and the uncertainty is \(\Delta A = \sqrt{\langle(\Delta\hat{A})^2\rangle} = \sqrt{\langle\hat{A}^2\rangle - \langle\hat{A}\rangle^2}\).

cards.title: What are the general and Heisenberg uncertainty relations?
cards.body: Any two Hermitian operators obey \(\Delta A\,\Delta B \ge \frac{1}{2}|\langle[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]\rangle|\); since \([\hat{X}, \hat{P}_x] = i\hbar\hat{I}\), position and momentum satisfy \(\Delta x\,\Delta p_x \ge \hbar/2\).
cards.tex: \Delta A\,\Delta B \ge \frac{1}{2}\left|\langle[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]\rangle\right|, \qquad \Delta x\,\Delta p_x \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}, \quad \Delta y\,\Delta p_y \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}, \quad \Delta z\,\Delta p_z \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}

ask.q: Since \(\Delta\hat{A}^\dagger = \Delta\hat{A}\), what does \(\langle\chi|\phi\rangle\) equal in Equation (2.100)?
ask.why: Because ΔÂ is Hermitian, ⟨χ|φ⟩ = ⟨ψ|ΔÂ†ΔB̂|ψ⟩ = ⟨ψ|ΔÂΔB̂|ψ⟩ = ⟨ΔÂΔB̂⟩.

ask.q: Why do \(\langle[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]\rangle\) and \(\langle\{\Delta\hat{A}, \Delta\hat{B}\}\rangle\) not cross-multiply in \(|\langle\Delta\hat{A}\Delta\hat{B}\rangle|^2\)?
options: One is purely imaginary and one is real
ask.why: Since [Â, B̂] is anti-Hermitian (purely imaginary expectation) and {ΔÂ, ΔB̂} is Hermitian (real expectation), |x + iy|² = x² + y².

steps.note: Equation (2.103): the squared modulus splits into the sum of two positive real squares.

ask.q: Since \(\frac{1}{4}|\langle\{\Delta\hat{A}, \Delta\hat{B}\}\rangle|^2 \ge 0\), what lower bound follows in Equation (2.105)?
ask.why: Combining Equations (2.101) and (2.104) gives ⟨(ΔÂ)²⟩⟨(ΔB̂)²⟩ ≥ ¼|⟨[Â, B̂]⟩|².

steps.note: Equation (2.106): taking the square root gives the minimum bound \(\Delta A\,\Delta B \ge \frac{1}{2}|\langle[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]\rangle|\).

ask.q: In Example 2.9, substituting \([\hat{X}, \hat{P}_x] = i\hbar\hat{I}\) into Equation (2.106) gives what?
ask.why: Since |⟨iħÎ⟩| = ħ, multiplying by ½ gives Heisenberg's uncertainty relation Δx Δp_x ≥ ħ/2 (Equation (2.107)).

steps.note: Equation (2.107): Heisenberg uncertainty relations \(\Delta x\,\Delta p_x \ge \hbar/2\) (and similarly for \(y, z\)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Equation (2.95), why does \([\Delta\hat{A}, \Delta\hat{B}]\) equal \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}]\)?
options: Because scalars \(\langle\hat{A}\rangle, \langle\hat{B}\rangle\) commute with all operators

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the general uncertainty relation between two Hermitian operators \(\hat{A}\) and \(\hat{B}\)?
cards.why: Equation (2.106) states that the product of uncertainties ΔA ΔB is at least ½|⟨[Â, B̂]⟩|.

cards.title: What is a function of an operator?
cards.body: A function \(F(\hat{A})\) of a linear operator \(\hat{A}\) is defined by the Taylor series \(F(\hat{A}) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n\hat{A}^n\); if \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = 0\), then \([\hat{B}, F(\hat{A})] = 0\).

cards.title: Adjoint and exponential relations (Equations (2.112)–(2.117))
cards.body: The adjoint of \(F(\hat{A})\) is \([F(\hat{A})]^\dagger = F^*(\hat{A}^\dagger) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n^*(\hat{A}^\dagger)^n\); when \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \ne 0\), \(e^{\hat{A}}e^{\hat{B}} \ne e^{\hat{A}+\hat{B}}\) and Equations (2.116)–(2.117) apply.

ask.why: Taking the adjoint conjugates the scalar a_n to a_n* and replaces Â^n with (Â†)^n.

ask.q: How is \(\sum a_n^* (\hat{A}^\dagger)^n\) written compactly in Equation (2.112)?
ask.why: Since the coefficients are conjugated to a_n* and the argument is Â†, the series is F*(Â†) (Equation (2.112)).

steps.note: Equation (2.112): even if \(\hat{A}\) is Hermitian, \(F(\hat{A})\) is Hermitian only if \(a_n\) are real.

ask.q: For \(F(\hat{A}) = e^{i\alpha\hat{A}}\) with complex \(\alpha\), what is \(a_n\) in \(\sum a_n\hat{A}^n\)?
ask.why: By Equation (2.109) with a = iα, the nth Taylor coefficient is (iα)^n / n!.

steps.note: Conjugating \((i\alpha)^n/n!\) gives \((-i\alpha^*)^n/n!\) in the series.

ask.q: What does the series \(\sum \frac{(-i\alpha^*)^n}{n!}(\hat{A}^\dagger)^n\) sum to in Equation (2.113)?
ask.why: By Equation (2.109), this is the exponential series for e^{−iα*Â†} (Equation (2.113)).

steps.note: Equation (2.113): when \(\alpha\) is real and \(\hat{A}\) is Hermitian, \((e^{i\alpha\hat{A}})^\dagger = e^{-i\alpha\hat{A}}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: If \(\hat{A}\) is Hermitian, when is \(F(\hat{A}) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n\hat{A}^n\) also Hermitian?
options: Only if all coefficients \(a_n\) are real
Only if all \(a_n\) are purely imaginary
cards.why: By Equation (2.114), [F(Â)]† = ∑ a_n* (Â†)^n = ∑ a_n* Â^n, which equals F(Â) only when a_n* = a_n (real coefficients).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is the commutator \([\hat{A}^n, F(\hat{A})]\) for any function \(F(\hat{A})\) of \(\hat{A}\)?
cards.why: By Equation (2.111), since Â commutes with itself, any power Â^n commutes with any function F(Â) of Â.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Equation (2.113), if \(\hat{A}\) is Hermitian, what is \((e^{i\hat{A}})^\dagger\)?
cards.why: By Equation (2.113), (e^{iÂ})† = e^{−iÂ†}, and since Â† = Â, this equals e^{−iÂ}.

cards.why: In Equation (2.109), e^{aÂ} = Î + aÂ + (a²/2!)Â² + ⋯ starts with the unit (or unity) operator Î for n = 0.

cards.title: Special directions that an operator only stretches or shrinks
cards.meaning: An eigenvector (or eigenket) |ψ⟩ of an operator Â is a special state that Â does not rotate into a new direction—it merely multiplies |ψ⟩ by a number a, called the eigenvalue.

cards.example: For the 2×2 matrix A = ((1,0),(0,-1)), the column (1,0)^T is an eigenket with eigenvalue +1, and (0,1)^T has eigenvalue -1.
cards.bridge: Section 2.4.8 writes the eigenvalue equation as Â|ψ⟩ = a|ψ⟩ in Equation (2.126) and establishes Theorems 2.1 to 2.5.

cards.title: What are eigenvalues and eigenvectors of an operator?
cards.body: A state \(|\psi\rangle\) is an eigenvector (eigenket or eigenstate) of \(\hat{A}\) with eigenvalue \(a\) if \(\hat{A}|\psi\rangle = a|\psi\rangle\); then \(F(\hat{A})|\psi\rangle = F(a)|\psi\rangle\) and \(\hat{A}^{-1}|\psi\rangle = \frac{1}{a}|\psi\rangle\).

cards.title: Theorems 2.1 & 2.2: Hermitian eigenvalues and eigenbasis
cards.body: Theorem 2.1: all eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator are real and eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal. Theorem 2.2: its eigenstates form a complete orthonormal basis where \(\hat{A}\) is diagonal.

cards.label: Proof of Theorem 2.1 · §2.4.8
cards.title: Proof of Theorem 2.1 (Equations (2.135)–(2.138))
cards.legend: \(\hat{A} = \hat{A}^\dagger\) Hermitian operator, \(|\phi_n\rangle, |\phi_m\rangle\) eigenvectors with eigenvalues \(a_n, a_m\).

phases.name: Action on ket
phases.why: project Â|φ_n⟩ = a_n|φ_n⟩ onto ⟨φ_m| in Equation (2.136)

phases.name: Action on bra
phases.why: project ⟨φ_m|Â† = a_m*⟨φ_m| onto |φ_n⟩ in Equation (2.137)

phases.name: Subtract & use Â = Â†
phases.why: obtain Equation (2.138): (a_n − a_m*)⟨φ_m|φ_n⟩ = 0

phases.name: Two cases
phases.why: set m = n for real eigenvalues and m ≠ n for orthogonality

steps.note: Equation (2.136): multiply \(\hat{A}|\phi_n\rangle = a_n|\phi_n\rangle\) on the left by \(\langle\phi_m|\).

ask.q: Taking the adjoint of \(\hat{A}|\phi_m\rangle = a_m|\phi_m\rangle\) gives what bra equation in (2.137)?
ask.why: By the Hermitian conjugate rule, (Â|φ_m⟩)† = ⟨φ_m|Â† and (a_m|φ_m⟩)† = a_m*⟨φ_m|.

steps.note: Equation (2.137): multiply \(\langle\phi_m|\hat{A}^\dagger = a_m^*\langle\phi_m|\) on the right by \(|\phi_n\rangle\).

ask.q: Since \(\hat{A}\) is Hermitian (\(\hat{A} = \hat{A}^\dagger\)), what does subtracting (2.137) from (2.136) give?
ask.why: With Â = Â†, the left sides ⟨φ_m|Â|φ_n⟩ and ⟨φ_m|Â†|φ_n⟩ cancel, leaving (a_n − a_m*)⟨φ_m|φ_n⟩ = 0 (Equation (2.138)).

steps.note: Equation (2.138): holds for any pair of eigenstates \(|\phi_n\rangle\) and \(|\phi_m\rangle\).

ask.q: In Case \(m = n\), since \(\langle\phi_n|\phi_n\rangle > 0\), what must hold?
ask.why: Because a nonzero eigenvector has ⟨φ_n|φ_n⟩ > 0, the factor (a_n − a_n*) must vanish, so a_n = a_n* is real.

steps.note: Case \(m = n\): all eigenvalues \(a_n\) of a Hermitian operator are real.

ask.q: In Case \(m \ne n\) with distinct eigenvalues \(a_n \ne a_m\), what follows from (2.138)?
ask.why: Since a_m is real (a_m* = a_m) and a_n ≠ a_m, dividing by (a_n − a_m) gives ⟨φ_m|φ_n⟩ = 0.

steps.note: Case \(m \ne n\): eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

cards.title: Theorems 2.3, 2.4 & 2.5: Commuting, anti-Hermitian, unitary
cards.body: Theorem 2.3: commuting Hermitian \(\hat{A}, \hat{B}\) (non-degenerate \(\hat{A}\)) share a unique common eigenbasis. Theorem 2.4: anti-Hermitian eigenvalues are purely imaginary or zero. Theorem 2.5: unitary eigenvalues have \(|a_n|=1\).

cards.label: Proof of Theorem 2.3 · §2.4.8
cards.title: Proof of Theorem 2.3: Joint eigenvectors (Equations (2.139)–(2.141))
cards.legend: \(\hat{A}, \hat{B}\) commuting Hermitian operators, \(|\phi_n\rangle\) non-degenerate eigenvector of \(\hat{A}\) with eigenvalue \(a_n\).

phases.name: Eigenvalue equation
phases.why: start with Â|φ_n⟩ = a_n|φ_n⟩ in Equation (2.139)

phases.name: Apply B̂ & commute
phases.why: act with B̂ and use B̂Â = ÂB̂ in Equation (2.140)

phases.name: Non-degeneracy
phases.why: deduce that B̂|φ_n⟩ is proportional to |φ_n⟩ in Equation (2.141)

steps.note: Equation (2.139): \(|\phi_n\rangle\) is the unique eigenvector of \(\hat{A}\) for non-degenerate \(a_n\).

ask.q: What do we get when we apply \(\hat{B}\) to both sides of \(\hat{A}|\phi_n\rangle = a_n|\phi_n\rangle\)?
ask.why: Since B̂ is a linear operator, it commutes with the scalar eigenvalue a_n.

steps.note: Apply \(\hat{B}\) from the left and pull the scalar \(a_n\) out in front.

ask.q: Since \([\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = 0\), how can we rewrite the left side \(\hat{B}\hat{A}|\phi_n\rangle\)?
ask.why: Because Â and B̂ commute, B̂Â|φ_n⟩ = ÂB̂|φ_n⟩ = Â(B̂|φ_n⟩) (Equation (2.140)).

steps.note: Equation (2.140): the ket \((\hat{B}|\phi_n\rangle)\) is also an eigenvector of \(\hat{A}\) with eigenvalue \(a_n\).

ask.q: Because \(a_n\) is non-degenerate, what does \(\hat{A}(\hat{B}|\phi_n\rangle) = a_n(\hat{B}|\phi_n\rangle)\) imply?
ask.why: Since |φ_n⟩ is the unique eigenvector for eigenvalue a_n up to a scalar multiple, B̂|φ_n⟩ must equal b_n|φ_n⟩.

steps.note: Equation (2.141): \(|\phi_n\rangle\) is simultaneously an eigenvector of \(\hat{B}\) with eigenvalue \(b_n\).

ask.q: What if \(a_n\) is a degenerate eigenvalue of \(\hat{A}\)?
options: A common eigenbasis still exists, but is not unique
ask.why: As noted below Equation (2.141), if one operator is degenerate, an infinite number of common orthonormal bases exist, so the joint basis is not unique.

steps.note: Both \(\hat{A}\) and \(\hat{B}\) are diagonal in the shared orthonormal basis \(\{|\phi_n\rangle\}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: If \(\hat{A}|\psi\rangle = a|\psi\rangle\) and \(\hat{A}^{-1}\) exists, what is the eigenvalue of \(\hat{A}^{-1}\) for \(|\psi\rangle\)?
cards.why: By Example 2.11 (Equation (2.134)), Â|ψ⟩ = a|ψ⟩ implies Â⁻¹|ψ⟩ = (1/a)|ψ⟩.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: According to Theorem 2.4, what are the eigenvalues of an anti-Hermitian operator?
options: Purely imaginary or equal to zero
cards.why: Theorem 2.4 states that the eigenvalues of an anti-Hermitian operator are either purely imaginary or equal to zero.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: According to Theorem 2.5, what is the modulus \(|a_n|\) of any eigenvalue of a unitary operator?
cards.why: By Theorem 2.5 (Equation (2.143)), a_n* a_n = |a_n|² = 1, so every eigenvalue of a unitary operator has modulus |a_n| = 1.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: By Theorem 2.2, a Hermitian operator is ______ when represented in its own orthonormal eigenbasis.
cards.why: Theorem 2.2 states that a Hermitian operator is diagonal in its eigenbasis, with diagonal elements equal to its eigenvalues.

cards.title: Turning kets, bras, and operators into columns, rows, and square matrices
cards.meaning: Once we pick a discrete orthonormal basis {|φ_n⟩}, every ket becomes a column of components, every bra becomes a conjugated row, and every operator becomes a square matrix.

cards.example: Inserting Î = ∑ |φ_n⟩⟨φ_n| in front of |ψ⟩ extracts the column entries a_n = ⟨φ_n|ψ⟩; inserting Î on both sides of Â extracts A_nm = ⟨φ_n|Â|φ_m⟩.
cards.bridge: Section 2.5.1 uses orthonormality ⟨φ_n|φ_m⟩ = δ_nm and completeness ∑ |φ_n⟩⟨φ_n| = Î to build matrix representations.

cards.title: What are completeness and the matrix representations of kets, bras, and operators?
cards.body: In an orthonormal basis \(\langle\phi_n|\phi_m\rangle = \delta_{nm}\) with completeness \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|\phi_n\rangle\langle\phi_n| = \hat{I}\), kets are columns \(a_n = \langle\phi_n|\psi\rangle\), bras are rows \(a_n^*\), and operators are square matrices \(A_{nm} = \langle\phi_n|\hat{A}|\phi_m\rangle\).

cards.title: What are the matrix adjoint, unitary matrix, and trace?
cards.body: The adjoint matrix is \(A^\dagger = (A^T)^*\) with \((A^\dagger)_{nm} = A_{mn}^*\) (Hermitian if \(A_{mn}^* = A_{nm}\)); a matrix is unitary if \(U^\dagger U = I\), and the trace \(\text{Tr}(\hat{A}) = \sum_n A_{nn}\) is cyclic: \(\text{Tr}(\hat{A}\hat{B}) = \text{Tr}(\hat{B}\hat{A})\).

cards.title: What is a change of basis and unitary transformation?
cards.body: Changing between orthonormal bases \(\{|\phi_n\rangle\}\) and \(\{|\phi'_n\rangle\}\) uses the unitary matrix \(U_{mn} = \langle\phi'_m|\phi_n\rangle\) (\(\hat{U}\hat{U}^\dagger = \hat{I}\)), transforming kets as \(|\psi_{\text{new}}\rangle = \hat{U}|\psi_{\text{old}}\rangle\) and operators as \(\hat{A}_{\text{new}} = \hat{U}\hat{A}_{\text{old}}\hat{U}^\dagger\).

cards.title: What are the secular equation and degeneracy?
cards.body: In a discrete basis, \(\hat{A}|\psi\rangle = a|\psi\rangle\) yields the secular (characteristic) equation \(\det(A_{mn} - a\delta_{nm}) = 0\); an eigenvalue shared by \(k\) independent eigenvectors is \(k\)-fold degenerate.

cards.label: Example 2.19 · §2.5.3
cards.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a 3×3 matrix (Equations (2.265)–(2.272))
cards.legend: Matrix \(A\) with \(A_{11}=7\) and lower \(2\times 2\) block \(\begin{pmatrix}1 & -i\\ i & -1\end{pmatrix}\), eigenvalues \(a_1, a_2, a_3\).

phases.name: Secular determinant
phases.why: expand det(A − aI) = 0 in Equation (2.265)

phases.name: Solve eigenvalues
phases.why: find the roots a₁ = 7, a₂ = √2, a₃ = −√2 in Equation (2.266)

phases.name: Eigenvector for a₂
phases.why: solve (A − √2 I)|a₂⟩ = 0 in Equations (2.269)–(2.270)

phases.name: Normalize |a₂⟩
phases.why: enforce ⟨a₂|a₂⟩ = 1 in Equations (2.271)–(2.272)

steps.note: Equation (2.265): expand the \(3\times 3\) determinant along the first row.

ask.q: Since \(i^2 = -1\), what does \([-(1 - a)(1 + a) + i^2]\) simplify to?
ask.why: -(1 − a²) − 1 = -1 + a² − 1 = a² − 2, giving (7 − a)(a² − 2) = 0 in Equation (2.265).

steps.note: Equation (2.266): the three eigenvalues are \(a_1 = 7,\ a_2 = \sqrt{2},\ a_3 = -\sqrt{2}\).

ask.q: For \(a_2 = \sqrt{2}\), the second row of \(A|a_2\rangle = \sqrt{2}|a_2\rangle\) in (2.269) is \((1-\sqrt{2})y - iz = 0\). What is \(z\)?
ask.why: From iz = (1 − √2)y, multiplying by −i gives z = -i(1 − √2)y = i(√2 − 1)y (Equation (2.270)).

steps.note: Equation (2.270): with \(x = 0\), the eigenvector has components \((0,\ y,\ i(\sqrt{2}-1)y)^T\).

ask.q: What does the normalization condition \(\langle a_2|a_2\rangle = |y|^2 + (\sqrt{2}-1)^2|y|^2 = 1\) give in (2.271)?

steps.note: Equation (2.271): sum the moduli squared of the components of \(|a_2\rangle\).

ask.q: Taking the positive root for \(y\), what is \(y\) in Equation (2.272)?
ask.why: Dividing by 2(2 − √2) and taking the positive square root gives y = 1/√[2(2 − √2)].

steps.note: Equation (2.272): substituting \(y\) completes the normalized eigenvector \(|a_2\rangle\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Example 2.14 (Equation (2.210)), what is the trace of any commutator \(\text{Tr}([\hat{A}, \hat{B}])\)?
cards.why: Because Tr(ÂB̂) = Tr(B̂Â) (Equations (2.208)–(2.209)), the trace of their difference Tr([Â, B̂]) = Tr(ÂB̂) − Tr(B̂Â) is always zero.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: Under a change of basis with unitary operator \(\hat{U}\), how does an operator \(\hat{A}_{\text{old}}\) transform?
cards.why: By Equation (2.239), under a change of basis kets transform as |ψ_new⟩ = Û|ψ_old⟩ and operators transform as Â_new = ÛÂ_oldÛ†.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: In Example 2.12, the ket \(|\psi\rangle = (5i,\ 2,\ -i)^T\) has norm \(\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\) equal to what number?

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: By Equations (2.260) and (2.261), the trace of a matrix equals the sum of its eigenvalues and the ______ equals their product.
cards.why: Equation (2.260) gives Tr(A) = ∑ a_n and Equation (2.261) gives det(A) = ∏ a_n.

cards.title: From discrete sums and Kronecker deltas to integrals and Dirac deltas
cards.meaning: When basis labels vary continuously (like position r or momentum p), sums become integrals and the Kronecker delta δ_nm becomes the Dirac delta function δ(k' − k).

cards.bridge: Section 2.6.1 replaces Equations (2.170)–(2.173) by the continuous Equations (2.275)–(2.278).

cards.title: What are a continuous basis and the Dirac delta function?
cards.body: A continuous basis \(\{|\chi_k\rangle\}\) satisfies \(\langle\chi_k|\chi_{k'}\rangle = \delta(k' - k)\) and completeness \(\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}dk\,|\chi_k\rangle\langle\chi_k| = \hat{I}\), where \(\delta(x - x_0)\) sifts out \(f(x_0)\) on \((a, b)\).
cards.tex: \langle\chi_k|\chi_{k'}\rangle = \delta(k' - k), \quad \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} dk\,|\chi_k\rangle\langle\chi_k| = \hat{I}, \quad \int_a^b f(x)\delta(x - x_0)\,dx = f(x_0)\ \ (a < x_0 < b)

cards.title: What are the position and momentum representations?
cards.body: In the position representation \(\hat{\vec{R}}|\vec{r}\rangle = \vec{r}|\vec{r}\rangle\), the component \(\langle\vec{r}|\psi\rangle = \psi(\vec{r})\) is the spatial wave function; in the momentum representation \(\hat{\vec{P}}|\vec{p}\rangle = \vec{p}|\vec{p}\rangle\), \(\langle\vec{p}|\psi\rangle = \Psi(\vec{p})\) is the momentum wave function.

cards.title: Connecting representations, Fourier transforms, and operators
cards.body: The transformation function \(\langle\vec{r}|\vec{p}\rangle = (2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}e^{i\vec{p}\cdot\vec{r}/\hbar}\) links \(\psi(\vec{r})\) and \(\Psi(\vec{p})\) as 3D Fourier transforms (Parseval's theorem preserves norm), giving \(\hat{\vec{P}} = -i\hbar\vec{\nabla}\) in \(\vec{r}\)-space and \(\hat{R}_j = i\hbar\partial/\partial p_j\) in \(\vec{p}\)-space.

cards.label: Derivation · §2.6.4.1 & §2.6.4.3
cards.title: Momentum operator P̂ = −iħ∇ and [X̂, P̂_x] = iħ (Equations (2.310)–(2.321))

phases.name: Insert momentum basis
phases.why: insert ∫ d³p |p⟩⟨p| = Î into ⟨r|P̂|ψ⟩ in Equation (2.310)

phases.name: Pull out gradient
phases.why: use p e^{ip·r/ħ} = −iħ∇ e^{ip·r/ħ} to get Equation (2.312)

phases.name: Act with X̂P̂_x and P̂_xX̂
phases.why: apply product rule to ∂(xψ)/∂x in Equations (2.318)–(2.319)

phases.name: Canonical commutator
phases.why: subtract to get [X̂, P̂_x] = iħ in Equation (2.321)

steps.note: Equation (2.310): insert \(\int |\vec{p}\rangle\langle\vec{p}|\,d^3p = \hat{I}\) and use \(\hat{\vec{P}}|\vec{p}\rangle = \vec{p}|\vec{p}\rangle\) and Equation (2.305).

ask.q: Which differential identity replaces \(\vec{p}\,e^{i\vec{p}\cdot\vec{r}/\hbar}\) in Equation (2.311)?
ask.why: Since ∇(e^{ip·r/ħ}) = (ip/ħ)e^{ip·r/ħ}, multiplying by −iħ gives p e^{ip·r/ħ} = −iħ∇e^{ip·r/ħ}.

steps.note: Equation (2.311)–(2.312): in position space, \(\hat{\vec{P}} = -i\hbar\vec{\nabla}\) and \(\hat{P}_x = -i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\).

ask.q: By the product rule in Equation (2.319), what is \(\hat{P}_x\hat{X}\psi(\vec{r}) = -i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x\psi(\vec{r}))\)?
ask.why: Differentiating the product xψ(r) with respect to x gives ψ(r) + x(∂ψ/∂x), yielding Equation (2.319).

steps.note: Equation (2.319): meanwhile \(\hat{X}\hat{P}_x\psi(\vec{r}) = -i\hbar x\frac{\partial\psi(\vec{r})}{\partial x}\) from Equation (2.318).

ask.q: When we subtract \(\hat{P}_x\hat{X}\psi(\vec{r})\) from \(\hat{X}\hat{P}_x\psi(\vec{r})\) in Equation (2.320), what remains?
ask.why: The derivative terms ∓iħx(∂ψ/∂x) cancel, leaving −(−iħψ(r)) = +iħψ(r) (Equation (2.320)).

steps.note: Equation (2.320): holds for every wave function \(\psi(\vec{r})\).

ask.q: In Example 2.20, what is \([\hat{X}, \hat{P}]\) when calculated in the momentum representation \(\hat{X} = i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial p}\)?
ask.why: Example 2.20 (Equations (2.327)–(2.329)) shows that [X̂, P̂] = iħ in both position and momentum representations.

steps.note: Equation (2.321): canonical commutation relation (generalized to \([\hat{R}_j, \hat{P}_k] = i\hbar\delta_{jk}\) in (2.324)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Equation (2.305), what is the transformation function \(\langle\vec{r}|\vec{p}\rangle\)?
cards.why: Equation (2.305) gives ⟨r|p⟩ = (2πħ)^{-3/2} e^{ip·r/ħ}, while ⟨p|r⟩ = ⟨r|p⟩* has a minus sign in the exponent (Equation (2.306)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: In the momentum representation (Equation (2.317)), what is the position operator \(\hat{X}\)?
cards.why: By Equations (2.316) and (2.317), in momentum space the position operator has a plus sign: X̂ = +iħ(∂/∂p_x).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: By Equation (2.326), what is the commutator \([f(\hat{X}), \hat{P}_x]\)?
cards.why: Equation (2.326) states that [f(X̂), P̂_x] = iħ df(X̂)/dX̂ (and [P̂, F(R̂)] = −iħ∇F(R̂)).

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: By Equation (2.309), ______'s theorem guarantees that if \(\psi(\vec{r})\) is normalized, its Fourier transform \(\Psi(\vec{p})\) is also normalized.
cards.why: Equation (2.309) proves that ∫ d³p Ψ*(p)Ψ(p) = ∫ d³r ψ(r)ψ*(r) = 1, known as Parseval's theorem.

cards.title: One eigenvalue equation Ĥ|ψ⟩ = E|ψ⟩, two famous languages
cards.meaning: Heisenberg's matrix mechanics and Schrödinger's wave mechanics are simply the discrete-basis and continuous-position-basis versions of the same equation Ĥ|ψ⟩ = E|ψ⟩.

cards.picture: Projecting Ĥ|ψ⟩ = E|ψ⟩ onto a discrete basis {|φ_n⟩} gives Heisenberg's matrix equation; projecting onto {|r⟩} gives Schrödinger's wave equation.
cards.example: Unitary transformations connect the two representations, proving that matrix mechanics and wave mechanics have identical physical content.
cards.bridge: Section 2.7 derives the matrix secular equation (2.352) in §2.7.1 and the Schrödinger differential equation (2.354) in §2.7.2.

cards.title: What is Heisenberg's matrix mechanics?
cards.body: Matrix mechanics represents \(\hat{H}|\psi\rangle = E|\psi\rangle\) in a discrete basis \(\{|\phi_n\rangle\}\) as \(\det(H_{mn} - E\delta_{mn}) = 0\); Heisenberg started from Bohr transition frequencies \(\nu_{mn} = (E_m - E_n)/h\) and non-commuting matrices.

cards.title: What is Schrödinger's wave mechanics?
cards.body: Wave mechanics represents \(\hat{H}|\psi\rangle = E|\psi\rangle\) in the continuous position basis \(\{|\vec{r}\rangle\}\) as \(\langle\vec{r}|\hat{H}|\psi\rangle = E\langle\vec{r}|\psi\rangle\), yielding the Schrödinger differential equation (2.354).

cards.label: Derivation · §2.7.2
cards.title: From Ĥ|ψ⟩ = E|ψ⟩ and de Broglie waves to Equation (2.354)
cards.legend: \(\hat{H} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 + \hat{V}(\vec{r})\) Hamiltonian, \(\psi(\vec{r}) = \langle\vec{r}|\psi\rangle\) wave function, \(\lambda\) wavelength, \(L = rp\) angular momentum.

phases.name: General eigenvalue problem
phases.why: start with coordinate-free Ĥ|ψ⟩ = E|ψ⟩ in Equation (2.351)

phases.name: Project onto ⟨r|
phases.why: write ⟨r|Ĥ|ψ⟩ = E⟨r|ψ⟩ in Equation (2.353)

phases.name: Position Hamiltonian
phases.why: substitute Ĥ = -(ħ²/2m)∇² + V̂(r) from Equation (2.315)

phases.name: De Broglie–Bohr link
phases.why: connect 2πr = nλ and λ = 2πħ/p to L = nħ

steps.note: Equation (2.351): general energy eigenvalue equation independent of any basis.

ask.q: How do we represent Equation (2.351) in continuous position space in Equation (2.353)?
ask.why: Projecting onto the position bra ⟨r| gives ⟨r|Ĥ|ψ⟩ = E⟨r|ψ⟩ (Equation (2.353)).

steps.note: Equation (2.353): here \(\langle\vec{r}|\psi\rangle = \psi(\vec{r})\) is the spatial wave function.

ask.q: By Equation (2.315), what is the Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}\) in the position representation?
ask.why: Since P̂ = −iħ∇, Ĥ = P̂²/(2m) + V̂ becomes −(ħ²/2m)∇² + V̂(r) in Equation (2.315).

steps.note: Equation (2.354): the time-independent Schrödinger equation of wave mechanics.

ask.q: In Section 2.7.2, substituting de Broglie's \(\lambda = 2\pi\hbar/p\) into \(2\pi r = n\lambda\) gives what?
ask.why: Replacing the electron's wavelength λ by 2πħ/p in the circular orbit condition 2πr = nλ gives 2πr = n(2πħ/p).

steps.note: An integer number \(n\) of de Broglie wavelengths fits around a circular orbit of radius \(r\).

ask.q: Multiplying \(2\pi r = n(2\pi\hbar/p)\) by \(p/(2\pi)\) yields which quantization rule?
ask.why: Canceling 2π and multiplying by p gives rp = L = nħ, which is Bohr's angular momentum quantization condition.

steps.note: Bohr's quantization condition \(L = rp = n\hbar\) reflects the uniqueness of the wave function on each orbit.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What was Heisenberg's starting point in formulating matrix mechanics (§2.7.1)?
cards.why: As explained in Section 2.7.1, Heisenberg started from Bohr's atomic transition relation ν_mn = (E_m − E_n)/h arranged in a square matrix.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How was the equivalence of matrix mechanics and wave mechanics proved (§2.8)?
options: Using the theory of unitary transformations
cards.why: Section 2.8 states that the equivalence between Heisenberg's matrix formulation and Schrödinger's wave formulation was proved using unitary transformations.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What form does \(\hat{H}|\psi\rangle = E|\psi\rangle\) take in the continuous position basis?
cards.why: By Equations (2.353)–(2.354), representing Ĥ|ψ⟩ = E|ψ⟩ in the continuous position basis yields the Schrödinger differential equation.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In matrix mechanics, physical quantities are represented by non-______ matrices, unlike classical mechanics where \(px = xp\).
cards.why: Section 2.7.1 emphasizes that matrix mechanics deals with non-commuting matrix quantities such as [X̂, P̂_x] = iħ.
